args.text:
Petrol ("gas") is sold by the gallon, at servos that are mostly self-serve (ya have to pump yer own) except for the ones in New Jersey, where self-serve is against the law, and in Oregon, where servos in the cities have to have at least 50% full-service pumps by law. The American gallon is smaller than the imperial gallon and comes to 3.785 litres.

Cos of all the "drive offs" during the crime waves of the 1990s and 2000s, near enough every American servo now makes drivers pay before they can pump (it used to be the other way round). These days, ya have to get a credit or debit card okayed at the pump first. Otherwise, ya have to guess how much petrol ya need, hand over that much of the folding stuff to whoever's on the till, and tell 'em which pump yer on (an American might say, "I need 50 bucks on pump number 1"). The pump'll cut out by itself when the petrol ya've put in hits the dosh ya handed over, or ya can go back and get a refund of any dosh ya didn't use if ya guessed too high.

The U.S. octane scale is different from the one used in Europe; a regular gallon of U.S. petrol has an octane rating of 87, about the same as 92 in Europe. In most states, servos give ya a choice of three grades of octane: 87 (regular), 89 (midgrade or plus), and 91 (premium). Unless yer hirin' a flash car, yer car'll most likely only need 87 (regular). If yer drivin' round the Rocky Mountains, ya might come across servos that sell petrol at lower octane ratings, mostly 85. That's fine for 87-octane cars up high, but if yer headin' down lower, make sure ya fill up with 87.

Diesel's not as common, but it's still used a fair bit and ya can get it at most servos, 'specially the ones that look after truckies. Untaxed "offroad diesel", sold out bush for farm use, is dyed red (and sometimes called "red diesel") and shouldn't go in cars, cos there's hefty fines if ya get caught.

In the United States, the old colour code at servos is that petrol comes out of nozzles with a black handle, and diesel comes out of nozzles with a green handle. That's the opposite of the colour code used in the United Kingdom. Don't mix 'em up.
